name: Chapter 7: Human Health and Disease
description: Common diseases and pathogens, malaria life cycle, immunity, vaccines, allergy, lymphoid organs, AIDS, cancer and drug abuse

cards.definition: Health = balance of certain humors (Hippocrates, Ayurveda); "blackbile" persons were hot and had fevers
William Harvey’s discovery of blood circulation and normal temperature in "blackbile" persons (thermometer)

cards.term: How does the mind affect health?
cards.definition: Through the neural and endocrine systems acting on the immune system
Genetic disorders, infections, life style (food, water, rest, exercise, habits)
A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being (not just absence of disease)
More efficiency and productivity, economic prosperity, longevity, lower infant and maternal mortality
Infectious: easily transmitted (e.g. AIDS, fatal). Non-infectious: not transmitted; cancer is the major killer.
Disease-causing organisms: bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoans, helminths

cards.term: Example of pathogen adaptation to the host?
cards.definition: Gut pathogens survive stomach’s low pH and resist digestive enzymes

Salmonella typhi: Typhoid; Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae: Pneumonia; Rhino viruses: Common cold; Plasmodium: Malaria; Entamoeba histolytica: Amoebiasis; Ascaris: Ascariasis; Wuchereria: Filariasis (elephantiasis)

cards.term: How does typhoid spread and where does it start?
cards.definition: Contaminated food and water; enters the small intestine, spreads through blood
Sustained high fever (39–40 °C), weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache, loss of appetite; severe: intestinal perforation
Widal test
Mary Mallon, a cook and typhoid carrier who spread it for years through food

cards.term: What does pneumonia infect, and effect?
cards.definition: The alveoli of lungs, which fill with fluid → severe breathing problems
Fever, chills, cough, headache; severe: lips and nails grey to bluish
Inhaling droplets/aerosols from an infected person, or sharing glasses and utensils
Dysentery, plague, diphtheria

cards.term: What does the common cold infect?
cards.definition: Nose and respiratory passage, not the lungs

cards.term: Symptoms and duration of common cold?
cards.definition: Nasal congestion and discharge, sore throat, hoarseness, cough, headache, tiredness; 3–7 days

cards.term: How does the common cold spread?
cards.definition: Droplets inhaled directly or via contaminated objects (pens, books, cups, doorknobs, keyboards)
P. vivax, P. malariae and P. falciparum
Plasmodium malariae
Malignant malaria by P. falciparum; can be fatal

cards.term: Infectious form of Plasmodium entering humans?
cards.definition: Sporozoites, via bite of infected female Anopheles
Multiplies in liver cells → attacks RBCs and ruptures them

cards.term: What causes the chill and fever in malaria?
cards.definition: Release of toxic haemozoin when RBCs rupture; recurs every 3–4 days

cards.term: Where do sporozoites form and get stored in the mosquito?
cards.definition: Formed after fertilisation in the mosquito’s gut; stored in the salivary glands

cards.term: Where does sexual reproduction of Plasmodium happen?
cards.definition: Gametocytes form in human RBCs; fertilisation occurs in the mosquito gut
Two: human and mosquito; female Anopheles is also the vector
"S into Human, G into Mosquito": Sporozoites enter humans; Gametocytes enter mosquitoes

cards.term: Where does Entamoeba histolytica live, and disease?
cards.definition: Large intestine; amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery)
Constipation, abdominal pain and cramps, stools with excess mucus and blood clots
Mechanical carriers: transfer the parasite from faeces to food
Internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia, blockage of the intestine
Eggs in faeces contaminate soil, water, plants; infection through contaminated water, vegetables, fruits
Wuchereria bancrofti and W. malayi
Slow chronic inflammation of lymphatic vessels of lower limbs (elephantiasis); genital organs also deformed
Bite of female mosquito vectors
Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton
Dry, scaly lesions on skin, nails, scalp, with intense itching

cards.term: Why does ringworm thrive in skin folds?
cards.definition: Heat and moisture (groin, between toes)
From soil, or using towels, clothes, comb of infected persons
Amoebiasis: Food/water contaminated with faeces (houseflies); Malaria: Bite of female Anopheles; Ascariasis: Water, vegetables, fruits with eggs; Pneumonia: Droplets, sharing utensils

cards.definition: Keeping body clean; clean drinking water, food, vegetables, fruits

Proper disposal of waste and excreta
cleaning and disinfecting water reservoirs, pools, tanks
hygiene in public catering
Avoid stagnant water, clean coolers, mosquito nets, Gambusia fish in ponds, insecticides, wire mesh on doors/windows
Dengue and chikungunya
Smallpox (declared eradicated by WHO in 1980)
Polio, diphtheria, pneumonia, tetanus

cards.term: How has biology helped control infectious diseases? (Exercise 2)
cards.definition: Vaccines, immunisation programmes, antibiotics and drugs, vector control, understanding of pathogens
Overall ability of the host to fight disease-causing organisms, conferred by the immune system
Non-specific defence present at birth; barriers to entry of foreign agents

Physical barriers: Skin; mucus of respiratory, GI, urogenital tracts; Physiological barriers: Stomach acid, saliva, tears; Cellular barriers: PMNL-neutrophils, monocytes, NK cells, macrophages; Cytokine barriers: Interferons from virus-infected cells

cards.definition: Secreted by virus-infected cells; protect non-infected cells from further viral infection
"Please Put Cats Carefully": Physical, Physiological, Cellular, Cytokine
Pathogen-specific and has memory
Primary: first encounter, low intensity. Secondary (anamnestic): later encounter, highly intensified.

cards.term: Cells carrying out acquired immune responses?
cards.definition: B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes

cards.term: Role of B cells vs T cells?
cards.definition: B cells produce antibodies. T cells do not secrete antibodies but help B cells, and mediate CMI.
Four peptide chains: two light, two heavy; H₂L₂

cards.term: Types of antibodies named in NCERT?
cards.definition: IgA, IgM, IgE, IgG

cards.term: Why is antibody response called humoral?
cards.definition: Antibodies are found in the blood (body fluid)

cards.term: Two types of acquired immune response?
cards.definition: Humoral (antibody-mediated, B cells) and cell-mediated (CMI) (T cells)
Cell-mediated immune response: body differentiates self from non-self

cards.term: What is checked before a transplant, and after?
cards.definition: Tissue matching and blood group matching; patient takes immunosuppressants lifelong
Host produces its own antibodies on exposure to antigens; slow, takes time for full effect
Immunisation (vaccine) and natural infection
Ready-made antibodies are given directly
Colostrum (IgA), antibodies via placenta to foetus, antitoxin, anti-venom

cards.term: Why is colostrum essential for newborns?
cards.definition: Abundant IgA antibodies protect the infant
Active: own antibodies, slow, long-lasting (vaccine). Passive: ready-made antibodies, fast, short-lived (colostrum, antivenom).
Innate: non-specific, from birth (skin, tears). Acquired: specific, with memory (antibodies, CMI).
The memory of the immune system
Antigenic proteins of the pathogen or inactivated/weakened pathogen
Generates antibodies and memory B and T cells that respond quickly and massively on later exposure

cards.term: When is passive immunisation used? Examples?
cards.definition: When a quick response is needed: tetanus antitoxin, snakebite antivenom
A preparation containing antibodies to the toxin
Large-scale production, greater availability; e.g. hepatitis B vaccine from yeast

cards.term: Why does a booster dose help? (intuition)
cards.definition: Each exposure re-trains memory cells, making the secondary response stronger and longer-lasting
Exaggerated immune response to certain environmental antigens (allergens)
IgE
Dust mites, pollen, animal dander
Sneezing, watery eyes, running nose, difficulty in breathing

cards.term: Chemicals released in allergy, and from which cells?
cards.definition: Histamine and serotonin from mast cells

cards.term: How is the cause of allergy found?
cards.definition: Exposing/injecting very small doses of possible allergens and studying reactions
Anti-histamine, adrenalin, steroids

cards.term: Why more allergies in metro children?
cards.definition: Protected environment early in life → lowered immunity and higher sensitivity
Body attacks self-cells due to genetic and unknown reasons
Rheumatoid arthritis
Lymphoid organs, tissues, cells and soluble molecules (antibodies)
Bone marrow and thymus: immature lymphocytes become antigen-sensitive
Spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer’s patches, appendix: lymphocytes meet antigens and become effector cells
Main lymphoid organ where all blood cells including lymphocytes are produced

cards.term: Location and change of the thymus?
cards.definition: Near the heart, beneath the breastbone; large at birth, shrinks to very small by puberty

cards.term: Where do T-lymphocytes develop and mature?
cards.definition: Bone marrow and thymus
Bean-shaped lymphocytes and phagocytes filters blood trapping microbes reservoir of erythrocytes
Trap microbes/antigens in lymph and tissue fluid; activate lymphocytes
Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue in lining of respiratory, digestive, urogenital tracts; ~50% of lymphoid tissue
MALT: Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue; CMI: Cell-mediated immunity; AIDS: Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome; NACO: National AIDS Control Organisation; HIV: Human Immuno deficiency Virus

cards.definition: Acquired: during lifetime, not congenital. Syndrome: a group of symptoms.
1981

cards.term: Update: NCERT says AIDS killed "more than 25 million". Current figure?
cards.definition: About 42 million deaths worldwide since the epidemic began (UNAIDS)

cards.term: What type of virus is HIV?
cards.definition: A retrovirus: envelope enclosing an RNA genome
Sexual contact transfusion of contaminated blood sharing needles infected mother to child through placenta
Multiple sexual partners, IV drug users, those needing repeated transfusions, children of infected mothers
No; only through body fluids; infected persons should not be isolated

cards.term: Time lag from HIV infection to AIDS?
cards.definition: Few months to many years, usually 5–10 years

cards.term: First cell HIV enters, and what happens?
cards.definition: Macrophages: RNA → viral DNA by reverse transcriptase, integrates into host DNA; macrophage becomes an HIV factory

cards.term: How does HIV cause immune deficiency? (Exercise 11)
cards.definition: It infects and destroys helper T-lymphocytes (TH) progressively; their number falls
Bouts of fever, diarrhoea, weight loss; opportunistic infections (Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi, Toxoplasma)
ELISA (enzyme linked immuno-sorbent assay)
Anti-retroviral drugs: only partially effective; prolong life

cards.term: Update: NCERT says death is inevitable with AIDS. Today?
cards.definition: With early, lifelong antiretroviral therapy, people with HIV can reach near-normal life expectancy; undetectable viral load means no sexual transmission
NACO (National AIDS Control Organisation) and NGOs

cards.term: Steps to prevent spread of HIV?
cards.definition: Safe blood from banks, disposable needles, free condoms, controlling drug abuse, safe sex, regular check-ups
"Don’t die of ignorance"
Contact with other cells inhibits uncontrolled growth; cancer cells have lost it

cards.term: How is a cancer cell different from a normal cell? (Exercise 12)
cards.definition: Lost contact inhibition and growth regulation divides uncontrollably forming tumours may invade and metastasise
Benign: confined, little damage. Malignant: neoplastic cells grow rapidly, invade tissues, starve normal cells, metastasise.
Cells sloughed from a malignant tumour reach distant sites via blood and start new tumours; most feared property
Physical, chemical or biological agents that cause neoplastic transformation
Ionising: X-rays, gamma rays. Non-ionising: UV. Both damage DNA.
Chemical carcinogens in tobacco smoke
Viral oncogenes: genes of oncogenic viruses. Cellular oncogenes (c-onc)/proto-oncogenes: normal cell genes that cause cancer when activated.
Biopsy and histopathology; blood and bone marrow tests for leukaemias
Suspected tissue cut into thin sections, stained and examined under a microscope by a pathologist
Radiography: X-rays; CT: X-rays to build a 3D image; MRI: Strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiation

advancedHtml.backHtml:
Cancer imaging

Uses?

RadiographyX-rays
CTX-rays to build a 3D image
MRIStrong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiation

cards.definition: Antibodies against cancer-specific antigens; molecular detection of genes for inherited susceptibility
Surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy and immunotherapy
Hair loss, anaemia

cards.term: What are biological response modifiers? Example?
cards.definition: Substances that activate the immune system against tumours; e.g. α-interferon
Tumour cells evade immune detection; immunotherapy "wakes up" the immune system
Opioids, cannabinoids, coca alkaloids (mostly from flowering plants, some from fungi)
Bind to specific opioid receptors in the CNS and GI tract

cards.term: What is heroin chemically, and its common name?
cards.definition: Diacetylmorphine; "smack": white, odourless, bitter crystals
By acetylation of morphine, from latex of poppy Papaver somniferum

cards.term: How is heroin taken, and effect?
cards.definition: Snorting and injection; a depressant, slows body functions
Cannabinoid receptors, mainly in the brain

cards.term: Source of natural cannabinoids and products?
cards.definition: Inflorescences of Cannabis sativa → marijuana, hashish, charas, ganja

cards.term: How are cannabinoids taken, and their effect?
cards.definition: Inhalation and oral ingestion; affect the cardiovascular system
Erythroxylum coca, native to South America
Interferes with transport of dopamine potent CNS stimulant (euphoria, energy) excess → hallucinations
Coke or crack; usually snorted
Atropa belladonna and Datura
Barbiturates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines (used for depression, insomnia)
Very effective sedative and painkiller after surgery

cards.term: When does drug use become abuse?
cards.definition: Taken for non-medicinal purposes or in amounts/frequency that impair physical, physiological or psychological functions
Heroin (smack): Papaver somniferum; depressant; Cannabinoids (charas, ganja): Cannabis sativa; cardiovascular effects; Cocaine (coke, crack): Erythroxylum coca; stimulant, blocks dopamine transport

cards.term: How long has tobacco been used?
cards.definition: More than 400 years; smoked, chewed or as snuff
Stimulates adrenal gland to release adrenaline and noradrenaline → raises BP and heart rate
Cancers of lung, urinary bladder, throat; bronchitis, emphysema, coronary heart disease, gastric ulcer
Oral cavity cancer

cards.term: Why does smoking cause oxygen deficiency?
cards.definition: Increases CO in blood, reducing haem-bound oxygen
12–18 years: both a period and a process; bridge between childhood and adulthood

cards.term: Causes of drug/alcohol use in youth (Exercise 17)?
cards.definition: Curiosity, adventure, experimentation, escape from problems, academic stress, "cool" image (media), unstable families, peer pressure
Psychological attachment to effects like euphoria and temporary well-being
Tolerance of receptors increases, so they respond only to higher doses

cards.term: Can a single use lead to addiction?
cards.definition: Yes; even once can be a forerunner
Body shows a withdrawal syndrome (anxiety, shakiness, nausea, sweating) if regular dose stops abruptly
Reckless behaviour, vandalism, violence; overdose → coma, death from respiratory/heart failure, cerebral haemorrhage

cards.term: Warning signs of drug abuse in youth?
cards.definition: Drop in academics, absence, poor hygiene, withdrawal, depression, aggression, changed sleep/eating, weight fluctuations

cards.term: Infections risked by IV drug users?
cards.definition: AIDS and hepatitis B (sharing needles)
Nervous system and liver (cirrhosis); harms foetus in pregnancy
Narcotic analgesics, anabolic steroids, diuretics, certain hormones
Masculinisation, aggressiveness, mood swings, abnormal cycles, facial hair, enlarged clitoris, deep voice
Acne, aggressiveness, smaller testicles, less sperm, kidney/liver dysfunction, breast enlargement, baldness, enlarged prostate
Severe acne and premature closure of growth centres of long bones → stunted growth

cards.term: Parenting linked to lower substance abuse?
cards.definition: High nurturance with consistent discipline

cards.term: Can friends influence drug use? Protection? (Exercise 15)
cards.definition:
Yes, via peer pressure.
Say no firmly, choose friends wisely, seek help from parents/teachers, channel energy into sports, music, yoga
